newsitem.title: USA: Report clears Prudential of obstructing justice.
newsitem.headline: Report clears Prudential of obstructing justice.

text.p: A court-ordered investigation into allegations of document shredding by a Prudential Insurance Co of America lawyer cleared the big insurer and its attorney of obstruction of justice allegations.
The investigation also found attorney Michael Barr did not violate professional or ethical rules of conduct.
But U.S. District Judge Alfred Wolin, in an opinion late Wednesday on a report of the investigation, criticized the Newark, N.J.-based insurer and its legal representatives for insensitivity.

"When viewed through the prism of propriety, it appears clear Prudential's senior management and its legal representatives failed to demonstrate the sensitivity that was required," Wolin said in the opinion.
"If Prudential's physical existence was assessed in biological terms, one would conclude that its chromosomal structure lacks a sensitivity gene," Wolin wrote.
However, Wolin took no action against the insurer on the matter.
"Because this court has no jurisdiction to sanction insensitivity, the court leaves the remediation to the court of public opinion," Wolin said.
Wolin earlier this month appointed attorney Justin Walder to investigate allegations of document shredding by Barr, a partner with the Chicago-based law firm Sonnenschein Nath & Rosenthal.
Sonnenschein is Prudential's top outside counsel defending the company against allegations of deceptive sales practices.
The company has agreed to pay at least $410 million to as many as 10.7 million policyholders to settle the class action suit. A settlement could cost the mutual insurer more than $1 billion.
Prudential has already been fined $1 million for its role in destroying documents relevant to the case.
Prudential has admitted that documents were destroyed in a Cambridge, Mass., office. Wolin also found cause for action in sales offices in Des Moines, Iowa; Jacksonville, Fla., and Syracuse, N.Y.
